      "title": "Getting the most out of Editoria11y v3",
      "description": "Drupal CMS's accessibility recipe \"just works\"...most of the time. When you want it to work better, you find that there are more than 130 fields spread across three settings tabs! Learn how we got here from the project lead, and get practical tips on configuration and customization.\n\n**Prerequisite**\n\nNone\n\n**Target Audience**\n\nAnyone who cares about quality assurance. Typically site owners, QA managers, and/or developers responsible for improving the site editing experience\n\n**Outline**\n\nEditoria11y was conceived as a deeply integrated Drupal accessibility checker in 2019:\n\n-- v1 introduced automatic, inline alerts for accessibility issues on published pages.\n\n-- v2 added an as-you-type checker for CKEditor and Gutenberg, as well as site-wide dismissals and reports.\n\n-- v3 work is currently focused on building a full quality assurance suite. There are already 3x as many checks as v2, and 3x as much to configure!\n\nWe will explore what a well-configured site looks like, and present best practices for your site settings and themes:  \n\n-- Preventing false positives and annoying or repetitive alerts.  \n\n-- Splitting configuration between content authors and developers.  \n\n-- Writing custom tests.  \n\n-- Optimizing tip placement for dynamic or clipped content.  \n\n-- Using the new report maintenance tools and crawlers.  \n\n-- Adding Views relationships to customize filters, reports and exports.  \n\n-- Integrating the European Commission's new \"AI: Editoria11y\" module.\n\nWe will end with a look at what’s next, and how the community can guide and contribute to this project's roadmap.\n\n**Learning Objectives**\n\nLearners should:  \n\n-- Be able to optimize their checker to catch the specific issues common to their theme and editors.  \n\n-- Know where to find documentation and code samples for extending and modifying the checker.  \n\n-- Not feel overwhelmed by 130+ fields spread across 3 configuration tabs!\n\n**Experience level**  \nAnyone",

      "title": "From Overwhelm to Opportunity: Designing a Personalised Career Journey for 350+ NHS Roles",
      "description": "How do you help someone choose a career when you offer 350 options? This talk shows how we turned overwhelming NHS career data into a guided, personalised journey ,using Drupal to model complexity and design for uncertainty.  \n\n**Prerequisite**\n\nNo specific prerequisites are required. Familiarity with CMS platforms and how digital teams use them to serve diverse user audiences will help attendees get the most from this session. Some experience with Drupal content modelling or UX design is beneficial but not essential.  \n\n**Target Audience**\n\nAnyone curious about how Drupal is used to solve real,world problems at scale, whether you work in development, design, strategy, or just want to see what a complex public sector Drupal project looks like in practice.  \n\n**Outline**\n\nHow do you help someone choose a career when you offer 350 options?  \n\nNHS Health Careers serves one of the UK's most diverse digital audiences, from a 14-year-old picking GCSEs to a clinician pivoting careers. With 350+ roles, 1,000+ courses, and five legacy sites being merged into one, the challenge wasn't building a platform. It was designing a system that helps people answer: \"What should I do with my life?\"  \n\nThis talk walks through how we approached that problem, and built the answer in Drupal.  \n\nWe'll cover how we structured complex content relationships to make personalisation possible, designed guided discovery tools that replace overwhelming choice with intentional journeys, and integrated an external career-matching quiz API for both anonymous and authenticated users.  \n\nThe result: a personalised careers hub with a gamified career planner, contextual content filtering, and a homepage that adapts to each user's goals, interests, and qualifications.  \n\nThe lessons are transferable:  \n\nStructure your content model before you design personalisation  \n\nReduce cognitive load; more options rarely mean a better experience  \n\nDrupal is strongest when it's modelling complexity, not just rendering pages  \n\nWhether you work in public sector, education, or any large-scale content platform, this session will show you how Drupal can turn structural complexity into human clarity.  \n\n**Learning Objectives**\n\nAttendees will see how:  \n\nDrupal's content modelling made personalisation possible ,How structuring careers, courses, and progression pathways as related entities gave the platform the foundation to serve each user differently.  \n\nDrupal powered guided discovery at scale ,How Search API, Solr, faceted filtering, and Paragraphs replaced 350+ career listings with intentional, contextual user journeys.  \n\nA custom Drupal module bridged an external career-matching API ,How we integrated the CASCAID quiz API for both anonymous and authenticated users, handling identity, session state, and frontend data delivery end-to-end.  \n\nDrupal enabled personalisation without AI ,How well-structured content and deliberate UX ,not machine learning ,powered a homepage and career planner that adapted to each user's goals and qualifications.  \n\nDrupal brought five legacy sites into one coherent platform ,How Drupal's flexibility and scalability made it the right choice for a public sector organisation managing a diverse, ever-growing national audience.\n\n**Experience level**  \nBeginner",

      "title": "Page Builder Deathmatch: Canvas vs Display Builder in a Real World Project",
      "description": "Canvas or Display Builder? Which one is the right tool for your job? And what may explode i if you install both?\n\n**Prerequisite**\n\nThe session is suitable for all experience levels:  \n\n- No prior knowledge of Canvas or Display Builder required: I start from zero and pull no punches  \n\n- I also don't assume you know the difference between slots and props, but the explanation will be very short\n\nWhat helps maximize your takeaways:  \n\n- Basic familiarity with Drupal's content model  \n\n- Knowledge of Drupal's theming or layout system (SDCs, layout builder, paragraphs, or block layout)  \n\n- Experiences with other page builders\n\n**Target Audience**\n\nDrupal developers, site builders, and technical architects evaluating modern page-building approaches for real projects. Ideal for teams working with Layout Builder, Paragraphs, or SDCs who need to decide between Canvas and Display Builder. Especially valuable for those responsible for architecture decisions, editor experience, and long-term maintainability in complex Drupal implementations.\n\n**Outline**\n\nTwo contenders. One Drupal site. And the wrong choice for your task can cost you  days or weeks.\n\nCanvas and Display Builder are both approaching production maturity. And both promise to revolutionize how editors, site builders, and designers work with Drupal. But they are built on fundamentally different assumptions, and choosing between them is a critical architectural decision.\n\nIn this session we put them through their paces across three rounds:\n\nRound 1: Page Layout  \n\nCan they replace Drupals fragmented theming approach consisting of block layout, theme regions and templates? What does setup actually involve, and what trade-offs emerge?\n\nRound 2: Managing Displays  \n\nHow do they handle Drupal’s data model (entities, fields, formatters, widgets) and map to component \"slots and props\"?\n\nRound 3: Frontpage Gauntlet  \n\nFlexible landing pages like a Frontpage require editorial autonomy, multilingual content, media handling, and AI-assisted workflows. Which approach works out with that?\n\nEach round is fought in real projects' requirements. Gotchas, workarounds, and limitations are pointed out. The session closes with a practical decision framework so you leave the arena knowing which tool is suitable for the given requirements of your next project and how upcoming roadmap developments may influence that choice.\n\nLet's get ready to rumble.\n\n**Learning Objectives**\n\nAfter this session, you have:  \n\n- A clear understanding of the underlying assumptions of Canvas or Display Builder  \n\n- A checklist to guide your next project decision  \n\n- Awareness of real-world pitfalls before you hit them\n\n**Experience level**  \nAnyone",

      "title": "The joy and power of SDC, finally for form inputs",
      "description": "We can never get enough of SDC, the front-dev friendly API to implement and share UI components for Drupal. So, let’s rejoice together by discovering the biggest improvement since the introduction of the API: we will soon be able to implement form elements directly with SDC, only with UI logic and front technologies, without messing with backend APIs.\n\nPierre, one of the maintainers of SDC in Core, will show you all the cool stuff which can be done with this addition.\n\n**Prerequisite**\n\nKnowledge about SDC and components-based theming.  \n\nAnd/or about Drupal Admin UI, especially display building tasks (Block Layout, Layout Builder, Views...)\n\n**Target Audience**\n\nFront developers, design system owners, ambitious site builders\n\n**Outline**\n\nThe introduction of SDC to Core in 2023 had a significant impact on the Drupal ecosystem by starting a movement to embrace design system methodology, helping the front-designers to implement ambitious shareable designs, and bringing display building back to the forefront.\n\nHowever, the UI components related to form inputs can’t be implemented as SDC yet and are still managed the old way, with abstruse PHP classes.\n\nDate picker, interactive data table, file uploader, slider, toggle, draggable tree view… they often constitute around 20% of design system scopes and their absence is felt heavily by project teams and the contrib space.\n\nGood news! We will land support to form elements in SDC in 2026 and it will be a game changer. Full component libraries will be packageable as Drupal themes and shared between projects, and front devs will finally get the full ownership of design implementations.\n\nIt will also be the opportunity to clean large parts of the rendering pipeline by finalizing the split between UI logic and business logic.\n\nWe will explore together how we can use those new UI components programmatically in front and back development.  \n\nAnd we will discover exciting demos about their use from Admin UI, leveraging them as Field Widgets to build an Entity Form Display.\n\n**Learning Objectives**\n\nHow to build and share UI components for form inputs  \n\nHow to use them in projects, both programmatically and from Admin UI\n\n**Experience level**  \nIntermediate",

      "description": "Drupal Commerce was developed from the ground up on Drupal 7, both benefiting from and contributing to the development of the Entity API, Views, and Rules modules. Its ecosystem of contributed modules supports recurring billing with all of its complexities in addition to complex tax, multilingual, multi-currency, and omnichannel configurations.\n\nMoving forward to Drupal 8, we're reevaluating our feature set and architecture to make Commerce easier to use and to develop for.       "title": "An Overview of the Drupal 8 Plugin System",
      "description": "Goodbye hook_block_info(), hello Block Plugins.\n\nThe Drupal 8 plugin system provides a set of guidelines and reusable code components that allow developers to expose pluggable functionality within their code and (as needed) support managing these components through the user interface. Understanding the ins and outs of the plugin system will be critical for anyone developing modules for Drupal 8. Blocks, field types, widgets, and views displays are just some of the places you’ll encounter plugins in D8.\n\nIn this presentation Joe will draw on [his experience working with Drupal 8 plugins](https://drupalize.me/blog/201409/unravelling-drupal-8-plugin-system) in order to write about and helping document the plugin system,  and walk through:\n\n- What are plugins and why, when, where are they used?\n\n- How Drupal discovers plugins.\n\n- Annotations and how they relate to plugins.\n\n- Defining a plugin.\n\n- Using plugin derivatives to allow for many instances of a single plugin.\n\n- Defining new plugin types in your own module.\n\nThis presentation will be useful for anyone who will be writing new Drupal 8 modules or porting existing code from Drupal 7 to Drupal 8.       "title": "Design Systems and Drupal",
      "description": "Modern Web design demands visual systems that ensure content is delivered to our myriad devices, from smartphones to tablets to desktop displays and beyond, in usable ways. It requires thinking in terms of content that gets presented, often in a variety of different ways, rather than simply presentation.\n\nDrupal has for years handled content independent of a particular design, in a sort of platonic content ideal.  That makes designing for a Drupal development project is a perfect fit  for design systems-thinking and results in greater efficiency and better quality. Using a smart design systems approach paired with good content strategy results in a project that fits amazingly well with Drupal's own design and capabilities... if we can recognize how to unify them.\n\nIn this session, Larry Garfield, Palantir's Senior Architect and Community Lead, will provide practical examples for how modern, modular design systems and practices can map directly to Drupal’s Views module, view modes, image styles, panels and other common site building tools.
